note: Vol. I No. 23. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST. THIS TRANSCRIPTION CARRIES ONE PRINTED PAGE TWICE AND ANOTHER NOT AT ALL: its block marked ISSUE PAGE 4 / SOURCE PDF PAGE 24 is a second reading of the same printed columns its ISSUE PAGE 2 block carries, verified column for column at four independent points — the steamboat explosion at page 2 column 1 lines 1442-1443 against page 4 column 1 lines 3549-3550; the 'CLINTON' canal letter at lines 2380-2381 against 4478-4479; the infant-school letter at 2394-2396 against 4490-4492; and the New York election squib at 2412-2431 against 4650-4654. The two readings are cut at different offsets and are therefore complementary, which is how claim c001 reads its salutation. The consequence is that this issue's printed page 4 is not in the transcription at all, and no claim here cites the page 4 block. Filed as its own ticket. Claims are otherwise from page 3, which carries the advertising.

claims.normalized: [MR. CALHOU]N, Sir,—On the evening of [the … inst. I wa]s present at the examination [of the INFANT] S[CH]O[OL] belonging to this town, emplo[yed …]
claims.notes: AN INFANT SCHOOL BELONGING TO THIS TOWN, WITH AN EXAMINATION HELD IN IT ONE EVENING IN THE SPRING OF 1834. A correspondent signing 'CANDOR' writes to the Democrat's editor about a public examination of the town's infant school — its 'amiable and accomplished teachers', their pupils' progress, and the objections some townspeople raise against infant schools generally. That is a schooling institution with a building, a staff of more than one, and an audience that turns out at night; and it is the third distinct schooling reference the corpus now holds inside seven months, after the school 'recently established in this village, by Mr. Sproat of Boston' (1833-11-26, claim c003) and School District No. [?]'s school house (1834-05-28, claim c013). NONE OF THE THREE IS PLACED and this pass does not join them to each other. THE EDITOR'S NAME IS SUPPLIED: the salutation reads 'iN, Sin,—' here and 'ALHOUN, Sin—-' in this issue's second reading of the same printed lines (page 4 column 7, line 4490), and John Calhoun is the Democrat's printer and editor, whose office the paper's own imprint puts on the corner of South Water and Clark (1833-11-26, claim c033).

claims.notes: 'OPPOSITE TO FORT DEARBORN' — the phrase in the earliest of the month's two readings, and the one where the anchor is nearly whole. The card is read at length from 1834-05-28 (claim c016 there), whose page 3 column 6 keeps the full reference list and 'his Wane House, opposite to' with the fort's name cut away; here the fort's name survives and the words before it are lost. Between them the sentence is 'his Ware House, opposite to Fort Dearborn', and neither reading could carry it alone. THE TRANSCRIPTION READS 'Port Dearborn' and the reading is Fort: there is no Port Dearborn in this corpus or on this lake, the P/F confusion is a recognition-class error, and the fort is the only structure of that name in the town. The line order in this column is scrambled by the segmenter — the agents' list, the goods and the dateline are interleaved with a neighbouring advertisement — so `lines_of_claim` names the whole block and the reading restores the sense without asserting an order the column does not have.

claims.notes: THE CORNER OF DEARBORN AND LAKE, SET AS A DISPLAY LINE, AND FIVE MONTHS EARLIER THAN THE CORPUS HAD IT. The same advertisement was read out of 1834-10-01 (claim c006 there) with the corner mangled to 'CORNER OF DEARBOEY AND LANE-STRENTS' and a dateline the reading had to correct from 'April 22, 1831' to 1834. THIS READING SETTLES BOTH: the display line is legible here as 'CORNER OF DEARBORN AND LAKE-s[treets]', and the dateline reads 'April 22, 1834' with the year intact, which confirms the correction made there on internal grounds alone. Botsford's tin and stove shop therefore stands at that corner from at least 22 April 1834 to 1 October 1834. Fullerton & Botsford sell pork at the same corner in the same run (1834-05-28, claim c007); the shared surname is recorded and NOT resolved.

For a reconstruction that has to decide how big a stick a Chicago builder could get, that is a direct answer from the market rather than an inference from surviving buildings: sixty feet is a warehouse or a bridge member, not a cabin, and fourteen inches square is heavy scantling. It sits with the same issue's price current, which lists 'Square timber, length' as a priced commodity (claim c010). THE PRICE IS NOT HERE and the notice gives none. 'Drills' is read for 'THRills' as a recognition error; the word is not certain and the reading marks it by bracketing the initial only.

claims.normalized: For Sale, [LOT] No 3, in Block 120, in the School Sec[tion.] For term[s enquire of] PR[U]YNE & CO.
claims.notes: A LOT AND A BLOCK NUMBER, NAMED, IN THE SCHOOL SECTION. This is one of the very few claims in the whole newspaper corpus that carries a surveyed address rather than a descriptive one: Block 120, Lot 3, School Section — Section 16, the school lands south and west of the original town, subdivided and sold from 1833. It does not say what stood on it, and nothing is built from it; what it establishes is that the School Section subdivision was being traded lot by lot in May 1834 by the same firm that kept a store between Clark and Dearborn (1834-05-21, claim c004). A house and land agent on Lake Street advertises twelve more building lots in the same section in the following week (1834-05-14, claim c002).

claims.notes: THE PROBATE COURT SITS AT THE JUDGE'S OWN OFFICE IN CHICAGO — 'at my office at Chicago' — and the notice is dated 2 May 1834. Three names attach: David Laughton, deceased and testate; Stephen Forbes, to whom letters testamentary are to issue, who is the same Forbes whose house on the west bank of the Des Plaines holds the county militia election a month later (1834-05-28, claim c009); and R. J. Hamilton, Judge of Probate for Cook county, who is the county's whole judicial establishment in these pages. A SECOND LAUGHTON ESTATE runs alongside it in the same column — Barnardus H. Laughton's, administered by Sophia Laughton — and the two are NOT joined: David and Barnardus H. share a surname and nothing here says they were kin.

Seven rows under one heading: assorted poplar lumber by the thousand feet, shingles the same way, square timber by the length, brick by the thousand, stone by the perch, lime by the barrel, wood by the cord. Every one of those is a material the reconstruction places, and the units are the ones the trade actually used. The right-hand fragments on two of these lines ('ver Chissols;', 'ca;', 'ane?') belong to Chase & Ballard's hardware list in the neighbouring physical column and are dropped by the reading. THE FIGURES ARE NOT CLAIMED: the price column is set in the next segmenter column and survives as a handful of numbers that cannot be attached to named rows without guessing, and this pass does not guess.

The reconstruction's siding, sheathing and shingle decisions rest on what timber was actually on the Chicago market in 1834, and this is the market speaking: pine and whitewood — that is, tulip poplar, the 'poplar ass'd' of the same issue's price current (claim c011) — in one yard, alongside flour from a stone mill. David Carver appears three times in this issue: here, in the marine list as a consignee (claim c013), and in a separate flour and oats notice. NO ADDRESS in any of the three.

claims.notes: A WOMAN TAKES OUT LETTERS OF ADMINISTRATION IN COOK COUNTY, MAY 1834, AND SIGNS FOR IT. Sophia Laughton administers Barnardus H. Laughton's estate; four weeks later she advertises the vendue of his personal property inside his own former dwelling house (1834-05-14, claim c004, and 1834-05-21, claim c017). The three notices together are the fullest sequence the corpus holds on any single Chicago household — a death, an administration, and a sale in the house. THE YEAR IS CORRECTED: the line reads 'J day of May, 1224', an impossible date on a paper that began in November 1833, and 1834 is the reading. The day of the month is cut away and is NOT supplied.
